analytical_question: As of 2026-10-13, can the hypothetical mid-sized food packaging manufacturer absorb, govern, and sustain synchronized digital twins of a manufacturing production line, specifically a read-only twin of one packaging line for maintenance planning with supervisors retaining every equipment decision? The immediate decision is preparation versus a bounded pilot within the case's next 6–12 months, not routine deployment. Maintenance staff, supervisors, operators, and the plant manager are affected. Existing human-directed maintenance is the implied comparator; its actual procedures and performance are not supplied. Separate offline retrospective assessment, non-influential shadow observation, and an operational advisory pilot. Automatic control, other lines, and wider deployment are excluded; long-range market forecasts are separate from this decision horizon.
general_et_finding:
ET generally — evidence boundary: E1 describes synchronized models and a need for validation; E2 describes security and trust concerns. Both are short case-supplied NIST summaries, not inspected originals. They establish topics relevant to technical capability and assurance, not adoption, performance, or a current market placement.
Diffusion population: For the underlying manufacturing-line technology, a proposed consistent adopter unit is a manufacturing production line with sustained use of a synchronized twin. The geographic market, dated numerator, addressable line population, observation period, and sustained-use criteria are not supplied. The broader manufacturing need and the narrower packaging-maintenance niche must be counted separately; no supported alternative denominators or counts permit sensitivity analysis. Diffusion stage not established, with very weak empirical adoption evidence. Neither innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority, nor remaining nonadopters can be assigned measured shares. Chapter 6's approximate category shares are theoretical reference points, not these market data.
Curves and influence: No cumulative-adoption series supports slow growth, acceleration, saturation, or a cumulative S-curve position. No period-by-period new-adopter series supports a bell-curve position; purchases, publicity, and sustained use cannot be substituted for one another. Neither Bass external influence nor peer-driven internal influence is established by observed adoption behavior. Bass estimate not supported; qualitative evidence used. No fitted coefficients, eventual market size, or threshold date is warranted. A curator-supplied, consistently defined dated series and reproducible fit would reopen this assessment, not automatically authorize adoption.
Landscape: Innovation Trigger is not established: no loaded breakthrough or demonstration trajectory. Peak of Inflated Expectations is not established: no publicity/success-and-failure series. Trough of Disillusionment is not established: no failures, backlash, or supplier-exit observations. Slope of Enlightenment is not established: no repeated operational benefit cases. Plateau of Productivity is not established: no routine-use and supplier-evaluation evidence. These missing observations prevent placement, rather than placing the technology at the beginning. No Gartner chart or reported placement is loaded. Silence is not steady coverage, and a neutral technical summary is not an adoption census. Supply dated use cases and coverage observations to change these findings.
General accelerator/inhibitor and timing: A model synchronized with a physical line is a potential learning opportunity inferred from E1, not measured diffusion acceleration. The strongest loaded general caution is the need for validation, reinforced by security/trust concerns (E1–E2); the scale of any adoption inhibition is unknown. These signals favor disciplined local preparation and evidence gathering, not waiting for an invented maturity date. The portfolio is incomplete: two summarized documents, one issuer/provenance group, no established recurring landscape trackers, no independent operational observations, no annual history. The local organization's resources cannot alter this external finding.
application_finding:
ET for this application — scope and fit: Read-only maintenance planning for one packaging line could reduce avoidable stoppages, but this is an unmeasured hypothesis. Model fit is explicitly unvalidated (E3). A demonstration, purchase, or approved trial budget is not operational success. Compare against existing human-directed maintenance; obtain its actual fault, intervention, and stoppage records before claiming incremental advantage. An offline retrospective test uses historical records without influencing work; shadow observation must likewise be isolated from live decisions. An operational pilot allows human reliance and requires a separate gate.
Application versus peer diffusion: The application population is packaging lines sustaining read-only twin-assisted maintenance; the relevant peer population is comparable mid-sized food-packaging manufacturers, using firms as the unit and a disclosed line-level scope. Geography, sustained-use counts, addressable populations, and observation periods are not supplied as of 2026-10-13. Diffusion stage not established for both, with weak evidence. The application's potential accelerator is its bounded advisory scope; its inhibitor is unproven maintenance utility. Comparable peers could supply practical social proof, but none is loaded; transferability and peer acceleration are unknown. Neither niche nor broader manufacturing adoption can be inferred. Timing implication: earn local learning while obtaining comparable peer evidence; do not use market labels to skip readiness gates.
Rogers attributes: Relative advantage — UNKNOWN. Fewer stoppages are desired, while intervention cost, missed faults, implementation effort, and ongoing support are unmeasured. Compare the same representative conditions against the baseline and count harmful recommendations as well as useful ones. Compatibility — MIXED. Supervisor authority is consistent with the stated nonautomatic scope, but actual routines, incentives, interfaces, and operator acceptance are unknown; map an alert-to-review workflow with users before live reliance. Complexity — INHIBITS as a risk inference. Synchronization, validation, troubleshooting, and continuing updates require work beyond viewing alerts; required skills and effort are not established. Demonstrate these tasks and support handover before operational use. Trialability — MIXED. One line, sensor history, protected engineer time, and a trial budget make limited offline preparation plausible; read-only output can still cause a human shutdown. Make the learning question, data permission, isolation, duration, fallback, and stop rule explicit before a test. Observability — UNKNOWN. No sustained outcome is supplied; avoided stoppages can be difficult to attribute. Share baseline-comparative fault/intervention records, review burden, and uncertainty with operators, maintenance staff, supervisors, and sponsor rather than displaying a model demonstration. Each attribute improves only with the corresponding measured outcome or accepted process.
Five individual stages: Knowledge — sponsor commitment indicates interest, not full understanding; engineer competence and supervisors'/operators' understanding of limits are unknown. Have each role explain the reliance boundary and practice failure cases. Persuasion — sponsor support is supplied, but maintenance, supervisor, and operator attitudes and trusted messengers are not; use user-selected peer reviewers and measured burdens/benefits to address false alerts and extra work. Decision — sponsor, protected time, and approved trial budget establish a commitment to learning, not complete authorization of a defined safe operational trial or users' acceptance. A signed owner-and-scope charter is needed. Implementation — no integrated real-work use, training completion, support, or procedure is established; supervisor capacity to review is insufficient proof. Demonstrate a working review and escalation rehearsal before reliance. Confirmation — no repeated value, continued use, bypass, or abandonment evidence is supplied; log outcomes and user feedback over a bounded evaluation before continuation. The immediate bottleneck is the transition from trial intent to accountable, governed implementation; confirmation remains a later gate.
Moore/Maloney: No base case identifies a real comparable organization, actual implementation, operational setting, measured outcome, and limitations. All those elements must be supplied to bridge capability to a solved maintenance problem. No vendor advocacy language or novelty-to-utility shift is loaded; the business-need statement is an organizational aim, not market social proof. The approximately 16% heuristic cannot substitute for missing populations or the chasm contract.
Ecosystem and implementation clock: Standards/interoperability are UNKNOWN: interfaces and required practices are not supplied, so inspect interface documentation before connecting anything. Complementary technological assets include the stipulated sensor history and the implied means of supplying synchronized data; actual access, infrastructure, synchronization, and quality are unverified. Complementary skills and review procedures are different assets and need assignments. No mass-adoption network effect is established for a single-line read-only model; local data/system participation is a dependency, not proof of a network effect. Supplier, product/form factor, support commitments, and viability are unspecified; do not equate the general category with a vendor. The 'horse' is unvalidated fit; the 'jockey' is unknown integration/support execution. Both need evaluation. Construction difficulty, infrastructure changes, specialized skills, complementary commitments, integration effort, and organizational absorption are not measured; the owner gap and validation work argue for prerequisite closure without inventing a duration from other technologies. No bottom-up user adaptation is reported; the chapter's top-down emphasis cannot establish whether users will reshape the application.
Chasm contract: A — NOT ESTABLISHED. No concrete operational use case is supplied, much less two independent origins showing repeatable relevant use. B — NOT ESTABLISHED. No temporal coverage observations establish a move from backlash to ordinary use. C — NOT ESTABLISHED. No trusted tracker's comparable consecutive annual editions or placements show movement closer. E1 and E2 share NIST provenance and supply none of those observations. CROSSING NOT ESTABLISHED — evidence is insufficient or unresolved. No affirmative contradiction supports a NOT CROSSED finding; missing evidence is not failure evidence, and the required five-to-six-tracker portfolio is unmet.
Forecast/lens comparisons: No old/new annual placements, same-label pair, direction, newer eligible reversal, or methodology history is loaded. Forecast movement is not assessable, rather than unchanged. Scope changes, changed anchors, renamed categories, removals, and retreat must be checked if editions arrive. No IEEE Computer Society evidence establishes commercial viability, humanitarian impact, market maturity, or adoption timeline separately. There is no supported Gartner/IEEE agreement or disagreement to average. Supply comparable editions and their methods before changing timing claims.
Alternatives/complements/competitors: The implied existing human-directed maintenance workflow is the supported baseline alternative; retain it while collecting its actual performance. Sensors/history are case-supported technological complements, with interfaces and synchronization still to verify. Other competing technical approaches, platforms, or supplier comparisons are not covered. Request a curated comparison; no unsupported product capability or superiority claim is made. Strongest application accelerator: a potentially bounded learning scope. Strongest inhibitor: unvalidated usefulness under false-alert/missed-fault consequences. These support preparation now, not live operational reliance.
organization_specific_finding:
PREPARE FIRST. Prepare ownership and the validation/reliance boundary now; hold the operational pilot. Sustained use is not ready because no continuing model-update owner is named. The following statuses concern this hypothetical case, not audited capacity (E3–E4); proposed owners and deadlines are recommendations.
Leadership and sponsorship — MIXED. Plant-manager sponsorship supports preparation now; authority detail, conflict resolution, business-outcome accountability, and continuing sponsorship are unestablished. Before the pilot, the plant manager should sign a scope/outcome charter and identify the escalation authority. Acceptance is documented decision rights and review commitment, including the post-pilot period; otherwise retain preparation only.
Skills and training — MIXED. Protected maintenance-engineer time is a strength; validation/integration competence, user interpretation skills, troubleshooting competence, and backup coverage are UNKNOWN. Before testing setup, the engineer and proposed operating owner should document task coverage; before reliance, supervisors/operators should demonstrate boundary and failure-case understanding. A task-and-training record and rehearsal, with unresolved tasks assigned, change this finding; protected time alone does not.
Workflow and process — MIXED. Supervisors can review alerts and retain decisions, but no review/escalation/error/fallback procedure is supplied. Urgent before any live influence: proposed supervisor lead, with maintenance and operators, drafts and rehearses triage, independent corroboration, logging, escalation, and return to baseline. Observed completion within available review capacity, including exceptions, is the gate.
Infrastructure and data — MIXED. Sensor history exists; its representativeness, quality, fault labels, timeliness, synchronization, interfaces, permissions, and read-only isolation are UNKNOWN. Model fit is separately unvalidated. During preparation the engineer and a proposed IT/access owner should produce a data/access assessment and technical validation protocol. No connection or performance inference is justified until access and isolation are demonstrated; suitable data and reproducible results would support the next phase.
Resources and budget — MIXED. Trial budget and protected time support bounded preparation; amounts, displaced work, integration/training cost coverage, continuing funding, and backup resources are not supplied. Plant manager should approve a capped preparation/test work plan now and a recurring support allocation before operational reliance. Acceptance is explicit capacity, cost responsibilities, duration, and a feasible support plan; a trial allocation cannot demonstrate sustainability.
Governance and risk — MIXED. Supervisor equipment authority is stipulated, not an entire control system. Access/change permissions, validation acceptance authority, incident handling, stopping, and rollback are UNKNOWN. Wrong alerts can trigger unnecessary shutdown or a missed fault. Proposed operating owner, supervisor lead, and IT/access owner should document and rehearse these controls before any operational pilot. The sponsor accepts residual risk; failure to demonstrate isolation or fallback keeps live use blocked.
Culture and change — UNKNOWN. No operator consultation, trust, incentive alignment, actual resistance, or acceptance evidence is supplied. During preparation, the proposed supervisor lead should involve an operator-selected peer representative and maintenance users in workload review and scenario testing. Acceptance evidence is recorded concerns, resolved workflow changes, and observed correct practice, not mere attendance. Unknown acceptance must not be described as proven resistance.
Operating ownership — GAP, the single binding readiness constraint. No named owner for updates after the pilot is an explicit absence. Plant manager should first appoint a continuing accountable role with update/change authority, protected time, support/vendor liaison, performance review, documentation, handover, continuity, retirement, and funding arrangements. Proposed timing: within 30 days. Signed acceptance of these duties and an identified backup/support route are required; the engineer or sponsor is not automatically that owner. Without this, sustained operation remains not ready and the operational pilot stays held.
Ranking and diagnostic separation: Ownership comes first because the work needs an accountable person to commission, accept, and maintain validation and controls. Fit is the next material uncertainty, not demonstrated technological failure: an accountable bounded test can resolve it. Reliance/access/workflow controls follow closely due to the stated harms; data/skills, recurring resources, and user acceptance must be resolved for their phase. The source portfolio is a separate evidence problem and does not erase the actual local gap. Strengths—sponsor, engineer time, history, review capacity, and trial budget—make preparation credible rather than requiring indefinite deferral.
Social mechanism: Mass-media exposure and interpersonal influence are not reported. No actual opinion leader, change agent, or change-agent aide is identified; plant-manager seniority does not establish peer credibility. A vendor implementer, if engaged, would have a promotional interest and would not supply independent proof. Proposed bridge: an operator-selected respected peer works with a supervisor and engineer to review concrete false-alert/missed-fault examples, then returns results to shift peers. Homophily within operator groups could support trust or reinforce an incumbent routine; heterophily between operators, engineers, supervisors, and IT could transmit useful information but needs translation. These are design inferences, not observed behavior. Check the path through scenario performance and, later, actual review/logging practice and feedback; identify a credible bridge before live use if none emerges.
Burden and posture: Engineer and future owner bear validation/update/support work; supervisors bear review work; operators may bear interruption and logging work; the sponsor allocates resources. Any benefit reaches plant operations and potentially staff through fewer avoidable stoppages, after a measured operating period, while preparation burdens arrive first. Give users scheduled time to review evidence, change the alert workflow, and see the same outcome and burden records as management. Fast follower is the stated management posture, not a Rogers category or proof of majority adoption. Resourced learning fits that posture, but absent durable ownership and external practical proof conflict with an assumption of ready-to-copy implementation. There is no evidence of fear of missing out or irrational resistance; professional advice follows the need and consequences.
Posture counterfactual — analytical, not a second observed firm: Holding technology, evidence, resources, and harms fixed, an innovator posture could favor earlier or more exploratory offline learning and tolerate uncertainty in benefit. It still yields PREPARE FIRST for the operational pilot because risk appetite cannot supply continuing ownership or remove harmful reliance. A conservative posture might wait for more peer evidence before later operational commitment, but neither counterfactual changes external diffusion, landscape, or chasm status.

contrary_evidence_or_limitations: Strongest single evidence FOR chasm crossing: No qualifying evidence supplied. E1 describes capability and validation, not a concrete sustained operational case; sponsor resources in E3 are local assumptions, not external proof.

Strongest single evidence AGAINST chasm crossing: No qualifying evidence supplied. E2 security/trust concerns do not affirmatively show a failed adoption transition. Missing use cases, coverage trajectory, and annual movement justify CROSSING NOT ESTABLISHED, not NOT CROSSED.

Strongest objection to PREPARE FIRST: E3 supplies sponsor, time, data history, review capacity, and budget, while E4 confines the application to read-only advice. Those strengths make a small test plausible now. They do not assign continuing update authority or define a non-reliance boundary; offline preparation captures learning without treating these missing conditions as fulfilled. A signed durable owner assignment plus a verified test/control plan would reverse the immediate action to bounded validation.

Portfolio/history limitation: E1 and E2 are two short summaries from NIST with case-reported dates, not five or six trusted trackers. Originals, cadence, verified latest status, operational origins, comparable annual history, and coverage series are missing. Unknown historical availability is not proof that history does not exist. No independent verification or external retrieval occurred.

STALE-QUICKLY: Any assertion that the case-reported 2026-07-20 NIST page or February 2025 IR is the latest guidance as of 2026-10-13 would be unsupported. Ask the curator for version histories and originals; their dated summaries remain useful only for their limited stated scope. No supported current market-stage, forecast, supplier-capability, or viability claim is available to refresh.

VENDOR-HYPE RISK: No specific vendor assertion is actually supplied, so there is no particular ROI, uptake, or performance quote to verify or repeat. The case instructs treating any future vendor claims as unverified; require measured records and independent origins before relying on them. The desired stoppage reduction is a hypothesis, not demonstrated ROI.

Organizational facts are hypothetical assumptions. Baseline performance, data suitability, staff competence, operator acceptance, continuing funding, and practical controls are not established. Neither these unknowns nor unvalidated model fit prove failure.

Historical course anecdotes are reasoning checks only. Visible versus delayed benefits motivates burden measurement; technical merit versus implementation motivates separate fit/support review. No historical adoption percentage, market outcome, or technology-specific clock is transferred to this case. Diffusion and hype patterns need not be inevitable.
confidence_and_uncertainty:
External landscape — LOW confidence in any empirical stage or timing claim; HIGH confidence that the loaded collection cannot establish crossing because all three tests and the portfolio remain unsupported. No factual market stage is assigned.
Application fit — LOW. Fit is expressly unvalidated; available history and bounded scope offer a test opportunity but no accuracy, outcome, workload, or superiority result. Representative retrospective comparisons could support or defeat the benefit hypothesis.
Organizational readiness — HIGH within the hypothetical stipulations that continuing update ownership is absent and that preparation resources exist; LOW for unreported competence, acceptance, controls, and sustained funding. Sustained operation is not ready because of the explicit owner gap, with other dimensions unresolved.
Immediate recommendation — HIGH within this scenario. PREPARE FIRST directly addresses a tractable explicit prerequisite while preserving learning. Appointment of a continuing resourced owner, an accepted protocol, verified non-reliance/access controls, and suitable data would justify proceeding to bounded validation. A demonstrated serious fit mismatch, unacceptable burden, or inability to establish capacity could instead justify stopping this route or deferring; none is currently demonstrated. Unknown market maturity alone does not require abandoning useful preparation.
value_opportunity_implication:
Hypothesis: Relative to existing human-directed maintenance, synchronized line information might help identify useful maintenance actions and reduce avoidable stoppages. No savings, fault-detection benefit, or return is established. Management and plant operations would receive any delayed continuity benefit; maintenance users and operators might also experience fewer disruptions, but they should confirm that value rather than have it assumed for them.
Work arrives first: the engineer and proposed continuing owner validate data/model behavior and maintain updates; supervisors review and document decisions; operators may supply context and bear unnecessary-intervention disruption; management bears the allocated cost. Record engineering/update time, review workload, unnecessary interventions, missed faults, and stoppage outcomes alongside the baseline. Offline findings show potential rather than causal avoided-stoppage benefits; a later controlled operational evaluation is needed for realized value. Let affected staff inspect the evidence and change burdensome steps during scheduled review time. Realization depends on useful fit, acceptable workflow burden, authorized controls, and sustained ownership/resources, not demonstration quality.
risk_governance_implication:
Stated harms are unnecessary shutdown and missed fault (E4). Inference: read-only output can still alter a supervisor's decision and cause either harm; human review reduces neither uncertainty nor exposure automatically. E2 only flags security/trust concerns; it supplies no specific mandatory control or legal requirement.
Existing case conditions: supervisors retain all equipment decisions and can review alerts; sponsor, engineering time, data history, and trial budget exist. Proposed conditions: plant manager appoints the continuing operating owner; a proposed IT/access owner verifies permitted data access and read-only isolation; supervisors and operating owner agree review, corroboration, escalation, update/change approval, performance review, support continuity, and retirement duties. These appointments and controls have not occurred.
Boundary: Permit only human-approved limited offline preparation on authorized records now; do not connect experimental outputs to operational decision channels. Any later shadow phase must keep outputs from influencing live equipment decisions. Before operational advice, demonstrate validated fit for the agreed scope, functioning review capacity and procedures, and a resourced support arrangement. Keep baseline maintenance running; do not suppress existing fault checks or replace equipment judgment with model output. No automatic actuation or scope expansion is authorized.
Stop/fallback: Proposed owner or supervisor pauses evaluation immediately if output reaches live decisions before authorization, access/isolation fails, data become unreliable, unaccepted errors or burdens appear, or update/support coverage lapses. Withdraw experimental advice, retain existing maintenance, log and review the event, and require sponsor-approved corrective evidence before restart. Management and supervisors retain risk acceptance and operating authority; this analysis itself authorizes no spending or implementation.
recommendation_management_implication:
PREPARE FIRST. Within the next 30 days, management should establish continuing model ownership and a documented validation/reliance boundary for the single packaging line; hold the operational advisory pilot while allowing specifically approved, isolated offline preparation within existing trial resources. The decisive gap is absent post-pilot update ownership, not an asserted market immaturity. Sustained use is not ready.
1. Appoint the accountable continuing owner — Plant manager (case sponsor; appointment duty proposed) should first obtain written acceptance of update/change authority, maintenance/support, performance review, handover, retirement, protected capacity, backup route, and recurring resource responsibilities (E3). Proposed deadline: day 30 from this decision. Acceptance evidence is a signed owner/support charter and resource plan. If absent, keep the pilot held; report the unresolved constraint at monthly sponsor review.
2. Establish a safe test plan and baseline — After owner assignment, the proposed operating owner, case maintenance engineer, proposed IT/access owner, and supervisor lead should document permissions, read-only isolation, non-reliance, baseline maintenance, escalation/fallback, representative data needs, and threshold-setting authority (E1–E4). Proposed deadline: day 60. Limited offline inventory/protocol drafting may occur sooner under sponsor approval; no live connection or reliance follows automatically. Acceptance is a checked data/access assessment, signed protocol, demonstrated isolation, and agreed stop rules. If unsafe or unsuitable, repair the plan/data or stop that test route.
3. Complete a bounded offline evaluation and workflow rehearsal — Under the approved plan, engineer evaluates and the continuing owner and supervisor lead review. Proposed review: within 90 days of setup approval, with an earlier stop for exposure or unacceptable results. Hypothesis: the twin adds maintenance-relevant information beyond the baseline without unacceptable false interventions, missed faults, review effort, or update burden. Use representative historical operating/fault conditions and a separately assessed comparison segment where available; document gaps rather than invent sufficient coverage. Evaluate technical errors, intervention implications, baseline comparison, review effort, and update/support work. Operators participate in scenario review and can propose changes. Before results are used, sponsor, owner, and supervisors must set acceptance thresholds covering harms, workload, coverage, and sustainment; no numerical limits or adequate sample size are supplied here. Insufficient coverage means inconclusive, not passed.
4. Make a recorded phase decision — Sponsor, with owner and supervisors, should review the package promptly after evaluation and within the case's 6–12-month pilot-decision horizon. Continue to a bounded non-influential shadow phase only if its ownership, data, isolation, budget, protocol, and review gates pass. Change the model/workflow for remediable failure; stop if useful fit or acceptable support cannot be demonstrated. Authorize an operational advisory pilot only after acceptable fit evidence, rehearsed reliance controls, documented user readiness, and continuing resources are accepted. Set its duration and outcome/stop rules before starting. Routine use and expansion require separate confirmation of repeated value and support; neither follows from an offline pass.
Why the strongest alternative loses: PROCEED WITH BOUNDED VALIDATION immediately would assume accountable continuing ownership and an adequate test/reliance boundary that the case does not provide. Preparation retains the benefit of the supplied resources without that assumption. DEFER AND MONITOR would underuse credible preparation capacity; rejection lacks evidence of substantive mismatch. These are recommendations for accountable human approval, not executed authorization.
change_monitoring_triggers: Ownership closure — Proposed owner: plant manager. Inspect signed owner/support charter and resource allocation at day 30 and monthly thereafter. If continuing update authority, capacity, acceptance, and continuity are documented, reopen bounded validation subject to remaining setup gates; if missing, continue PREPARE FIRST and keep operational use held.

Fit and burden — Proposed owners: maintenance engineer as evaluator, continuing owner and supervisor lead as reviewers. Inspect baseline-comparative evaluation log at each test review and at the proposed 90-day endpoint after setup approval. Pre-agreed errors, missed-fault coverage, unnecessary-intervention implications, review effort, and update burden must pass; pass supports the next bounded phase, remediable failure changes the design, substantive failure stops it, and insufficient data remain inconclusive.

Reliance breach or resource deterioration — Proposed owners: supervisor lead and continuing owner, escalated to plant manager. Inspect incident/access logs during every test session and capacity/update records monthly. Unauthorized operational influence, failed isolation, unreliable data, missed updates, or lost support capacity pauses the affected phase immediately and retains baseline maintenance until corrected and reapproved.

Independent use-case corroboration — Proposed owner: human source curator with operating-owner review. At monthly preparation reviews and before major commitments, inspect any newly loaded operational case records for a real comparable organization, actual use, outcome, limitations, and independent origin. Two qualifying origins reopen Test A and transferability assessment; syndicated vendor stories do not. Adverse relevant cases revise the protocol or commitment, not automatically the whole technology judgment.

Coverage transition — Proposed owner: curator. Review dated longitudinal coverage collection quarterly, distinguishing enthusiasm/backlash, ordinary use, and missing coverage. An evidenced transition to sustained ordinary use reopens Test B; sustained contrary coverage requires inspecting actual failures. Neither one neutral article nor silence passes the test.

Forecast movement and contrary evidence — Proposed owner: curator.
